questions.question: What did the group discuss about the trend of teacher recruiting and the reasons for it, and steps they had taken?
questions.reference_answer: Although there were no exact figures,they had seen over recent years that they were only recruiting to about 65 percent of targets. It was partially due to the financial incentives, but that was not all of the problems. Because this issue was not only in Wales, but a common issue in all over the world. For example, in England, despite higher financial incentives to join ITE courses, people still were not getting onto those courses. To solve this problem, they had taken several steps including making sure their ITE provision was world class, embarking on the first national ITE recruitment marketing exercise, etc. In this process, Llyr Gruffydd had a doubt that the level of ambition did not reflect the level of action that was needed actually. Kirsty Williams responded that different statistics told different stories. They obviously understood there were many steps they had to take, but they were trying instead of just sitting back and waiting.

oracle.answer: The group discussed the trend of teacher recruiting, noting a significant challenge in attracting individuals to enter the teaching profession, with recruitment rates falling short of targets at approximately 65%. This issue is not unique to Wales but is observed globally, with similar challenges in countries like the USA, England, and Finland. Reasons for this trend include a lack of financial incentives being the sole solution, as well as broader systemic issues affecting potential teachers' perceptions of the profession. Steps taken to address this include improving Initial Teacher Education (ITE) provision, offering financial incentives, launching a national ITE recruitment marketing campaign, and setting up an advisory board on recruitment and retention. Additionally, efforts are being made to diversify the teaching workforce by encouraging career changers and implementing part-time PGCE routes to accommodate various life circumstances. Regarding Welsh language teaching, there is recognition of the need to maintain and enhance Welsh language skills among teachers, with plans to develop intervention programs and ensure consistent data collection on linguistic abilities.

questions.question: Summarize their discussion on the decision of not accrediting the University of South Wales with the ability to deliver teacher training.
questions.reference_answer: Kirsty Williams firstly made it clear that it would not be appropriate to comment this since this process was independent of Government. Hefin David then proposed the impact on students and staff. Kirsty Williams thought there would be a responsibility upon the University of South Wales to ensure that those students already in the system were able to complete their studies with the appropriate level of support and tuition to enable them to achieve their career aspirations and graduate from that program. The same was true for staff. Kirsty Williams thought that would be a matter for the institution. After this, they had some discussions on the geographic spread of provision.

Kirsty Williams, AM, stated that the decision-making process is independent of the government and expressed confidence in the EWC's appointed assessors. She acknowledged potential impacts on students and staff but emphasized that the government will commission sufficient training places from accredited institutions. For students currently enrolled at USW, she assured that the university must provide adequate support for them to complete their studies. Regarding staff uncertainty, Williams noted that such matters are the responsibility of the autonomous institution. An ongoing appeals process was mentioned, with a possible decision next month. Williams also highlighted the geographical spread of current providers and introduced a part-time PGCE route to address accessibility issues for students.

questions.question: Summarize their discussions on university mergers.
questions.reference_answer: Kirsty Williams firstly proposed that the main goal he would like to pursue was a healthy, strong and sustainable HE sector. They did not pursue or urge a policy of mergers, but they welcomed the mergers, if this was beneficial for individual institutions. Hefin David proposed that was in contrast with the predecessors, and talked about the situation when Cardiff Metropolitan University was under pressure from the previous Minister to merge with the University of Glamorgan and Newport. Kirsty Williams thought they needed to look at the future instead of looking at the past. They had a strong institution in Cardiff Met now. However, it was obvious that they got to learn some lessons from that process.

oracle.answer: Kirsty Williams expressed that she does not have a formal policy for university mergers but supports a sustainable higher education (HE) sector where institutions can choose to collaborate or merge if they see mutual benefit, prioritizing student interests. She clarified that there is no current government pressure to push for mergers, contrasting with previous approaches. She acknowledged potential disruptions to staff and students during such processes and emphasized the importance of learning from past experiences of reconfigurations. Williams stated that while she has no immediate intention to change her stance, unforeseen circumstances could necessitate a merger in the future.

questions.question: How did Kirsty Williams respond to university mergers?
